simple.     The  confusion  at  the  basis  of  Neumark's  misapprehension 

is  that  he  does  not  see  that  Aristotle's  analysis  of  natural  facts  is 

very  frequently  based  upon  an  analysis  of  what  is  implied  in  speech, 

a  method  he  must  have  inherited  from  the  Socratean  tradition.    In 

this  particular  case,   the  very  same  fact,   namely  the  yeveoig 

of  fiovGixog  äv&Qcojtog  as  suecceding  a  stage  of  äfiovöog  avQ-Qcojioq, 

is    expressed    in   language    in    two    ways   (1)    ö  av&gconoq  yivtxat

povoixog,  (2)  6  äfiovöog  yivsrat  ;iovoixog.  Which  of  these  twa 
represents  the  fact  more  precisely?  What  is  it  in  fact  which 
becomes  (lovöixög,  the  man  or  the  äfiovoog?  Aristotle  answers 
unequivocally,  the  man,  because  the  man  persists  in  both  stages. 
The  first  expression  therefore  is  the  more  precise  of  the  two.  But 
the  second  also  is  not  a  fiction,  it  also  represents  some  reality, 
namely  the  real  fact  that  the  man,  who  is  the  real  subject  of  the 
yhsöig,  had  as  his  ovfißsßrjxog  originally  the  negative  property 
(öTEQrjCig)  of  äfiovoog.  In  a  sense  therefore  (xara  övfißsßrjxog) 
we  may  say  that  the  äfiovoog  becomes  fiovöixog,  thongh  in  reality 
the  cqwvoog  becomes  nothing,  it  just  ceases  to  be.  This  two-fold 
aspect  of  viewing  any  given  process  of  ytrsoig  applies  to  all  kinds 
of  ytrsoig.  Now  we  are  ready  to  understand  what  Aristotle  means 
in  the  above  passage,  and  what  Simplicius  means.  They  both  have 
in  mind  expression  number  one,  which  is  the  precise  description 
of  the  process  of  ytrsoig,  in  as  much  as  it  names  the  two  principles 
or  elements  which  enter  the  product,  namely  matter  and  form. 
The  product  in  every  kind  of  yevedig  is  composed  of  matter  and 
form  x«#'  avro,  and  not  xara  av(ißeßi]x6g.  The  relation  of 
ortQ?/oig  to  the  product  is  xara  övfißeßrjxog,  because  it  really 
does  not  contribute  anything  except  its  absence  and  the  fact  that 
it  must  have  been  present  originally,  otherwise  there  would  have 
been  no  yivsöig  at  all.  This  is  the  meaning  of  Aristotle,  that  if 
we  consider  only  the  essential  elements  in  yiveoig,  we  have  only  two, 
matter  and  form.  This  is  true  of  every  kind  of  ytrsoig,  yivsöig 
ajiXmg  as  well  as  ytrsoig  rig.

Neumark  wants  to  know  why  the  thing  defined  cannot  be  used 
in  the  definition?  The  question  is  rather  amusing,  Coming  as  it 
does  from  one  who  volunteers  unsolicited  Information  about  the 
nature  of  "Analogieschluß",  etc.,  but  the  answer  is  provided  in  the 
longer  passage  from  the  Topics,  tov  yao  fiad-sZv  xdoiv  djzoöidorcu 
to  löiov  '  ccito  fihv  avTcö  ofiolmg  ayvcoözov  sötl.  Substitute 
Xoyog  or  oQioiwc  for  löiov,  and  you  have  the  reason  why  no 
definition  must  contain  the  thing  defined.  Let  us  hope  too  that 
Neumark  will  not  think  henceforth  that  the  Interpretation  I  gave 
is  "indiskutabel".  Alexander  and  Bonitz  may  both  be  wrong  and 
Neumark  may  be  right,  but  what  these  two  agree  in  saying  is  at 
least  "diskutabel",  with  Neumark's  permission. 

It  is  a  sufficient  criticism  of  Neumark's  Interpretation  of  Z  4. 
p.  1029  b  22—1030  a  3  that  it  reads  into  Aristotle's  words  what 
they  do  not  contain,  not  to  speak  of  the  fact  that  the  argument  is 
not  at  all  improved  thereby.  For  whether  we  analyze  Ifidnov  or 
do  not  analyze  it,  the  same  fact  remains  that  white  is  an  addition. 
The  Interpretation  of  Alexander  and  Bonitz  is  decidedly  the  correct 
one  of  the  text  we  have,  because  they  endeavour  to  make  the  text 
speak  for  itself,  and  if  the  result  is  not  satisfactory.  Neumark's  is 
still  less  so.  We  shall  therefore  be  on  safer  ground  if  we  follow  Alexan- 
der as  he  is  followed  by  Bonitz  and  Schwegler.  I  repeat  once  more 
that  while  the  interpretation  of  Neumark  is  untenable  enough  in 
the  entire  passage,  it  becomes  absolutely  impossible  in  the  simple 
sentence,  dXXd  r©  iiiarlro  eivcu  acta  iori  vi  t)v  eivai  vi  [)]]  oXcoq 
?j  ov:  The  text  is  here  uncertain  and  the  punctuation  varies  in

it  than  that  it  is  a  question,  "Is  there  a  vi  r\v  elvat  of  ifidnov  or 
not?"  I  cannot  see.  It  would  take  too  long  to  quote  Alexander

the  interested  reader  to  the  original  sources.

a  Xoyog  unfolds  an  ovofta  to  make  it  a  opia/soc,  for  if  that  were

every  örofta  and  an  örofia  for  every  Xoyog,  hence  the  Iliad,  too, 
i.  e.  the  epic,  would  be  a  definition,  for  it  is  a  Xoyog  signifying  the  same

If  Neumark  were  as  sensitive  to  the  rules  of  Greek  grammar 
and  lexicography  here  as  he  was  before,  he  would  have  known  that 
the  words  ov  sötI  tovto  to  rrcifrog  cannot  be  translated,  "von 
dem  jenes  nur  ein  Zustand  ist",  that  to  rrt'frog  cannot  be  a  predicate

exprcss  Neumark's  thought  the  phrase  would  have  to  be  oi  IotI 
exsivo  üta&oq,  or  ov  IotI  tovto  rrdfrog  without  the  article  (two 
mss.  du  omil  the  article).  Again  Öt/Xcöoai  does  not  mean  "in 
die  Erscheinung  treten",  but  "to  make  clear",  "to  explain", 
"erklären",  as  Bonitz  has  it.  Again,  taking  Neumark's  interpretation 
together  with  the  example,  the  Statement  would  be  that  the  coneept 
or  the  name  "female"  necessarily  belongs  to  "animai",  which  is  not 
true.     Animai  need  not  be  female,  it  may  be  male.     Neumark  adds

in  brackets  "[oder  Männliche]",  but  Aristotle  does  not  say  it.  Be-

(b  1),  ut  quid  sit  rectum  et  circulare  definiri  nequeat,  nisi  lineae  no- 
tione,  de  qua  illa  preaedicantur,  utaris  eamque  ad  definitionem  ad- 
hibeas".  In  other  words,  xad-'  avxd  predicates  are  those  in  whose 
definitions  the  subjects  in  which  they  inhere  are  implied  or  expressed. 
Thus,  straight  and  circular  are  xad-'  avxd  predicates  of  line,  because 
in  defining  straight  and  circular,  the  subject  line  must  be  expressed 
or  implied,  neither  straight  nor  circular  can  be  defined  without  re- 
ference  to  line.  White  is  not  a  xad-'  aixo  predicate  of  man,  because 
in  defining  white,  man  is  neither  expressed  nor  implied,  white  can 
be  defined  without  reference  to  man.  In  our  passage  of  the  Meta- 
physics,  aifiov,  (xqqev,  loov  are  xafr'  avxd  predicates  of  qiq,  £cöov, 
Jtoöov  respectively.  Aristotle  characterizes  them  in  the  phrase  above

The  two  interpretations  are  therefore  quite  different,  the  only

r  ovo'  äv  jtots  eylvsro,  si  ol'rojg  ?}v,  rods  xi  cannot  possibly 
mean,  "would  not  all  things  of  the  same  class  be  completely  equal." 
sylvsTO  refers  to  yivsöig,  not  to  the  form  which  things  would 
take  after  yivsöig.  xods  xi  means  a  particular,  and  a  particular 
is  not  the  same  as,  but  different  from,  any  other  particular.  The 
word  "all"  or  "all  of  the  same  class"  is  absolutere  essential  and 
it  is  not  in  the  text.  Moreover,  what  does  Neumark  do  with  the  word 
jioxs?  It  has  no  place  in  his  translation  at  all.  "Sometimes",  it  would 
have  to  mean,  but  the  qualification  would  make  no  sense.  In  my 
translation  ovo'  .  .  .  jioxs  means  "never",  and  gives  good  sense. 
The  correct  translation  is  therefore  the  one  which  I  gave,  and  which 
corresponds  to  that  of  Bonitz,  "Wenn  es  sich  so  verhielte,  so  würde 
nicht  einmal  ein  einzelnes  Etwas  entstehen".  And  Alexander  under- 
stands  it  exactly  in  the  same  way.  The  question  only  is  why  would 
yivsöig  of  the  particular,  hence  all  yivsöig,  be  impossible  on  this 
theory?  Alexander  gives  two  reasons.  Jirst,  if  the  Ideas  or  forms 
are  actual  and  separate  existences,  then  the  only  way  anything  could 
arise  from  matter  and  form  would  be  by  composition  {övvd-söig) 
and  not  yivsöig,  just  as  stones  become  a  house,  not  by  yivsöig, 
but  by  övvd-söig.  The  example  seems  to  nie  an  unfortunate  one. 
for  the  stones  of  a  house  are  not  the  form  but  the  matter.  However, 
the  idea  seems  clear,  he  wants  to  illustrate  that  yivsöig  is  not  the 
combination  of  two  actualities,  but  of  a  potential  and  an  actual.

Putting  the  Interpretation  of  Aristotle's  text  aside,  the  argument 
which  Neumark  brings  forward  against  the  Ideas,  taken  in  itself, 
does  not  appeal  to  me.  Why,  if  there  are  Ideas,  must  all  men,  say,

to  Aristotle's  conception  of  Plato,  is  a  real  thing  existing  in  an  in- 
telligible  world,  and  serving  as  a  model  for  the  things  in  this  world.

when  it  is  the  cause  of  the  production  of  a  natural  object,  Plato  now- 
here  makes  clear.  What  (leß-Egig  means  we  do  not  know.  We 
do  know  that  the  Idea  is  eternal  and  unchanging.  It  seems  to  me 
therefore  quite  possible  that  the  reason  Aristotle  says  here  that  on 
the  theory  of  Ideas  yeveoig  would  be  impossible  is  this  very  thing, 
namely,  how  can  a  thing  which  does  not  come  in  contact  with  its 
product,  and  remains  eternally  the  same,  not  being  in  any  way  affected

for  its  product,  or  be  a  cause  at  all?    However,  be  that  as  it  may,

Matter  and  Form    in  Aristotle.  67 

is  ambiguous,  and  was  used  in  two  different  senses  in  the  above  illu- 
strations.  And  the  reason  the  word  "part"  is  ambiguous  is  because 
the  word  "thing",  or  "circle",  or  "syllable"  is  also  ambiguous.  When 
we  speak  of  a  circle  we  may  mean  the  form  of  circle  as  the  geometer 
uuderstands  it,  or  the.  actual  line  merely  that  the  child  sees,  or  in 
a  cruder  sense  still  the  brass,  if  the  circle  is  made  of  brass.  Simi- 
larly  when  we  think  of  man,  we  may  think  of  that  which  makes  him 
man,  namely  his  soul  (containing  life  and  reason),  or  his  body  (flesh 
and  blood  and  bones),  or  the  man  as  a  whole,  soul  and  body.  Now 
just  as  when  we  think  of  man  we  may  have  any  one  of  those  in  mind, 
ho  when  we  think  of  part  of  man  (or  of  part  of  circle),  we 
may  mean  part  of  his  soul,  or  part  of  his  body,  or  part  of  the  com- 
posite  {jitQoq  iilr  ovv  eörl  xal  tov  tidovq  ....  y.ai  tov 
GvvdZov  tov  ex  tov  slöovq  xal  t/jj:  vZfjQ  xal  ryg  vk?]q  aw/jg). 
This  is  the  Solution  of  the  difficulty.  The  concept  denotes  the  form, 
that  we  know  already,  hence  the  parts  of  it  must  denote  parts  of 
the  form.  The  answer  then  is,  if  by  part  of  the  thing  you  mean 
part  of  the  form  of  the  thing,  then  it  is  true  that  the  concept  of  the 
part  of  the  thing  must  constitute  a  part  of  the  concept  of  the  thing, 
but  if  you  mean  by  part  of  the  thing,  part  of  the  matter  of  the  thing, 
then  the  concept  of  the  part  of  the  thing  does  not  form  part  of  the 
concept  of  the  thing.  Applying  our  result  to  the  above  illustrations, 
we  see  why  the  concept  of  semicircle  is  not  contained  in  the  definition 
of  circle,  because  a  semicircle  is  a  part  of  the  matter  of  the  circle, 
not  of  its  form.  But  the  concepts  of  vowel  and  consonant  are  con- 
tained in  the  concept  of  syllable,  because  vowel  and  consonant  are 
parts  of  the  f  o  r  m  of  syllable.

To  understand  the  meaniag  of  the  passage,  we  must  consider 
the  other  dizoola,  which  is  closely  related  to  the  first,  namely  are 
tlie  parts  always  prior  to  the  whole  or  not?  For  example,  is  an 
acute  angle  prior  to  a  right  angle?  Evidently  not,  for  in  defining 
it,  we  make  use  of  a  right  angle  in  our  definition,  saying  it  is  less 
than  a  right  angle.  Henee  the  latter  is  prior.  And  yet  in  some 
cases  the  parts  are  prior,  for  example,  animal  is  prior  to  man,  for 
man  presupposes  animal,  whereas  animal  does  not  presuppose  mar. 
This  djtoQia  is  solved  in  the  same  way  as  the  first  by  distinguishing 
the  different  meanings  of  the  word  part.  Parts  of  the  matter  are 
posterior  to  the  whole,  parts  of  the  form  are  prior  to  the  whole.  This 
Solution  he  illustrates  in  Irving  beings.  The  soul  is  the  form,  hence 
the  parts  of  the  soul  are  prior  to  the  ovro/.ov.  But  the  body  and 
its  parts,  as  being  matter,  are  posterior  to  the  ovoia.  Some 
material  parts,  however,  are  prior  to  the  ovvoXov  and  others  are 
simultaneous  with  it,  as  for  example  those  material  parts  which  are 
the  seat  of  the  soul,  like  the  heart  or  the  brain. 

This  passage  as  being  an  illustration  in  natural  things  of  the

understood  as  referring  not  to  the  universal,  but  to  the  particular,

we  actually  see  circles  of  other  materials  also,  viz.  stone  and  wood, 
which  shows  that  the  essence  of  circle  is  independent  of  brass.  Bnt

always  in  the  same.  we  are  apt  to  mistake  the  matter  for  form,  as 
for  example  in  man.  flesh  and  bones  are  the  only  material  in  which 
man  appears,  yet  it  is  elear  that  flesh  and  bones  do  not  belong  to 
the  form,  but  to  the  matter,  just  as  the  brass  of  the  circle  wonld  be 
none  the  less  matter  even  if  all  circles  were  of  brass.  The  moral 
of  this  remark  is  that  we  mnst  be  careful  not  to  be  misled  by  the 
constancy  of  the  material  of  a  given  thing,  and  mistake  it  for  form. 
On  the  other  hand  it  wonld  be  jnst  as  mistaken  to  go  to  the  other

storie  in  circle.  and  flesh  and  bones  in  man.  which  are  undoubtedly 
matter,  to  relegate  everything  to  matter  which  is  not  pnrely  abstract

asseverantis'1        Bo  litz  ad  A,  5,  987  a  26].    Now  he  says  some  thing 

eise.     Not  only  has  a  thing  its  proper  matter  but  there  may  be  several 

proper  matters  of  the  same  thing,  not  simultaneously,  however,  but 

so  that  one  of  these  is  the  matter  of  the  other,  thus  both  the  fat  and 

the  sweet  are  matters  of  phlegm,  but  in  such  a  way  that  the  sweet

is  the  matter  of  the  fat.  Phlegm  may  in  fact  still  have  a  third  matter, 
namely  gall,  but  this  not  in  the  regulär  progress  of  nature,  for  gall

in  an  indirect  way,  by  first  being  resolved  into  the  .-rQcoTtj  vXtj,  and 
then  in  the  regulär  progress  of  nature  pass  through  the  sweet  and

namely  the  same  matter  may  become  the  material  of  different  things,

some  cases  this  is  impossible,  for  cxample  a  saw  cannot  be  made

than  one  material,  the  efficient  cause,  in  the  sense  of  the  art,  must 
be  the  same.  For  when  both  the  matter  is  different  and  the  art 
is  different,  the  produet  too  would  be  different. 

The  matter  is  quite  clear  now.  Aristotle  is  not  at  all  trying

which,  however,  are  not  incompatible  with  it.  Xeumark,  however,

These  insinuations  are  really  too  contemptible  to  deserve  an 
answer.  But  I  shall  answer  them.  I  did  not  either  in  this  passage 
or  in  any  other  depend  upon  translations,  and  used  them  either  not 
at  all,  or  very  sparingly.  I  did  use  very  diligently  the  original  text 
of  Aristotle  and  the  commentaries  of  Alexander,  Simplicius,  and 
Bonitz.  Now  and  then  I  also  consulted  Zeller,  von  Hertling,  Baeumker, 
Schwegler,  Philoponus,  Themistius,  etc.  If  Neumark  instead  of 
using  three  translations  had  consulted  the  Greek  commen- 
tators  and  Bonitz  and  Schwegler  diligently  and  modestly,  he 
would  not  have  gotten  into  trouble.  In  the  present  passage  I  used 
no  translation  whatsoever,  and  did  not  find  the  Euclid  citation  any- 
where  outside  of  Euclid,  nor  did  I  see  any  reference  to  it  anywhere. 
The  reason  I  cited  Euclid,  I  could  have  proved  my  point  from  Aristotle 
just  as  well,  is  because  I  wanted  to  make  it  clear  that  the  terms  oyjjita 
kjthteöov  are  used  here  in  their  technical  mathematical  sense,  and

§  31.  I  hope  I  have  now  fnlly  justified  my  original  eriticism  of 
Neumark's  Aristotclian  chapter  in  the  first  volume  of  his  history  of 
Jewish  Philosophy,  if  there  was  a  doubt  hitherto  in  the  minds  of  those 
able  to  judge.  That  Neumark  cannot  take  objeetive  eriticism  gracefully 
and  must  needs  reduce  the  matter  to  the  low  level  of  personal 
abuse  and  mean  insinuation  is  to  be  regretted.  But  since  he  has 
foreed  me  to  go  into  the  subject  at  such  great  length,  and  once  more 
In  make  a  study  of  the  parts  of  his  book  involved,  I  think  I  am  en- 
titled  to  teil  him  a  few  piain  truths,  not  at  all  in  a  spirit  of  bravado 
or  of  personal  triumph,  but  in  a  serious  and  objeetive  manner.  I 
shall  try  my  best  not  to  exaggerate.  The  chapter  in  question  is 
a  failure.  This  I  have  proved  abundantly.  But  apart  from  that 
it  has  no  place  in  his  book.  If  Neumark  had  original  views  to  pro- 
pound  on  matter  and  form  in  Aristotle,  his  book  on  Jewish  philo- 
sophy was  not  the  place  for  it,  and  his  manner  of  presentation  not 
the  proper  one.  No  Aristotelian,  I  mean  scholars  like  Diels,  Baeumker. 
von  Arnim,  Rodier,  to  speak  of  living  men  only,  looks  for  critical 
interpretations  of  Aristotle  in  a  history  of  Jewish  medieval  philo- 
sophy. On  the  other  han  1  the  ordinary  Student  or  reader  of  Jewish 
philosophy  knows  his  Aristotle,  if  he  knows  him,  chiefly  at  second 
band,  and  has  not  the  time  to  make  a  deep  study  of  the  sources. 
Neumark  himself  must  know  that,  for  he  himself  did  not  find  time 
to  study  the  Greek  cnmmentators.  His  views  on  Aristotle  and  his 
original  interpretations  he  should  have  discussed  eritieally  and  in 
detail  in  connection  with  the  Greek  text  and  with  direct  and 
c  on  s  t  a  n  t  reference  to  the  ancient  and  modern  cnmmentators, 
from  whom  as  I  shnw  he  differs  radically.     This  should  have    been

contributed  to  a  periodical  like  the  "Archiv"',  or  published  in  book 
form  under  a  title  which  would  have  called  the  attention  of  specialists 
to  its  existence.  Neumark  might  then  have  liad  the  benefit  of  the 
opinions  of  these  men.  On  the  other  hand  for  the  readers  and  stu- 
dents  of  his  book  what  was  needed  was  not  a  translation  and  lengthy 
discussions  of  selected  passages  from  the  Physics  and  Metaphysics 
of  Aristotle.  but  a  summary  view  of  Neumark's  resnlts  in  a  clear  and 
eoncise  manner  with  a  reference  to  the  teehnical  study  for  verification. 
As  it  is,  the  chapter  in  qnestion  is  a  misfit.  The  reader  interested 
in  Jewish  philosophy  is  quite  bewildered  and  actnally  repelled.  Tliis 
is  dne  to  a  great  extent  to  the  method  Neumark  has  chosen  for  pre- 
senting  his  Aristotelian  views,  thongh  not  a  little  of  the  trouble  is 
also  to  be  ascribed  to  Neumark's  st}ie  in  general.  He  lacks  clear- 
ness  of  thought,  perspicuity  of  style  and  conciseness  of  exposition. 
not  to  speak  of  his  faulty  and  nnreliable  jndgment.  He  possesses 
a  stupendoiis  amount  of  eruditiou,  and  a  measure  of  originality  and 
insight,  but  he  laeks  the  crowning  virtne  of  the  true  scholar,  modesty. 
and  wants  to  grasp  too  mnch.  If  he  would  only  submit  modestly 
to  the  guidance  of  such  competent  leaders  in  the  study  of  Aristotle 
as  I  mentioned  time  and  again  in  the  course  of  this  article.  instead 
of  haukering  for  original  views  and  should  continue  this  process 
of  training  for  several  years,  he  would  be  the  first  to  retract  his  un- 
fortunate  chapter. 

The  discussion  is  now  finished  so  far  as  I  am  concerned.  I  shall 
not  reply  to  any  further  Communications  of  Neumark  on  this  suh- 
ject.  I  hope,  however.  that  those  readers  of  the  "Archiv"  who  have 
followed  this  discussion  by  reason  of  their  interest  in  the  subject 
matter,  and  who  have  views  to  express  which  are  based  on  a  first 
hand  study  of  the  sources  involved.  will  not  hesitate  to  express  them- 
selves  in  public  on  the  merits  of  this,  to  the  end  that  those  not  so 
qualified  may  learn  from  the  expression  of  authoritative  opinions.
